official_metadata.abstract: Procedural memory in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems typically caches reusable multi-step action sequences, or skills, indexed by surface task features within a single task domain. This domain-siloed indexing leaves structurally transferable skills invisible to retrieval whenever a new task falls outside the domain in which the skill was originally cached, forcing redundant skill re-discovery, while naive cross-domain retrieval that ignores this structure risks negative transfer by applying an inappropriate skill without adaptation. This paper proposes Cross-Domain Skill Transfer (CDST), a procedural-memory mechanism that encodes cached skills both by surface features and by a domain-invariant structural schema, predicts transfer utility with a learned Transferability Estimator before attempting reuse, adapts a transferred skill’s domain-specific parameters through a slot-filling module, and promotes repeatedly successful transfers to a re-indexed meta-skill tier. CDST is evaluated on SciSkill-Transfer-90, a 90-instance benchmark spanning six directed domain-transfer pairs across three scientific-reasoning domains, against domain-siloed, naive cross-domain, and structural-similarity-only baselines. CDST achieves a target-domain task success rate of 87.9%, exceeding the strongest structural baseline by 11.1 percentage points, reduces the negative-transfer rate to 3.4% from 14.2%, and raises the skill reuse rate to 76.8%, a 27.9-percentage-point improvement over naive cross-domain transfer. Complexity analysis, an ablation study, a sensitivity analysis over the structural-similarity floor, and a scalability study over skill-cache size are reported, together with a qualitative case study and an explicit discussion of threats to validity.

official_metadata.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are promising in Internet of Things (IoT) applications. However, existing agent systems suffer from an ephemeral limitation: agents are instantiated for individual tasks and terminated upon completion, losing valuable execution experiences across different tasks where past knowledge reuse is impossible. Inspired by dual-process theory in cognitive science, we propose a brain cognition-inspired dual-system agent framework for continuous knowledge reuse across heterogeneous task streams, termed the cognition-inspired dual-system agent framework for continuous knowledge reuse (CIA-CKR). The CIA-CKR framework separates fast (reactive execution) from slow (deliberative planning) cognition phases by maintaining a persistent knowledge base throughout the operational lifetime of agents. Two synergistic mechanisms are designed that mirror bidirectional knowledge flow in human cognition: a personalized agent generation mechanism that retrieves task-relevant knowledge and configures context-specific agent capabilities through top-down adaptation, and a knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts experiential insights from execution traces through bottom-up feedback. Extensive experiments on HomeBench (smart home control) and OmniEAR (embodied multiagent collaboration) datasets demonstrate that CIA-CKR consistently outperforms both vanilla LLMs and recent memory-augmented methods, achieving 10.82% and 4.23% average accuracy improvements on HomeBench and OmniEAR, respectively, over the best baselines.
